course.title: Data Analysis with Python
course.tagline: Turn raw data into charts, reports and answers with Python, pandas and real datasets.

days.title: What Data Analysis Is and Your Toolkit
days.goal: Understand what a data analyst does and set up Python, pandas and Jupyter.

video.title: Data Analysis with Python for Excel Users - Full Course

steps: Install Python, then install pandas, numpy and matplotlib with pip.
Install Jupyter Notebook with pip install notebook and launch it with jupyter notebook.
Make a new notebook and run print('Hello, data!') in a cell.
Import pandas as pd and numpy as np in a cell and check they load without errors.
days.task: Set up your toolkit and run a notebook that prints the versions of pandas and numpy.
days.challenge: Open a notebook and try running a cell, then re-running it after changing the code.

quiz.q: What does a data analyst do?
options: Turns raw data into answers, charts and reports that help people decide
quiz.explain: A data analyst cleans data, explores it, finds patterns and explains what it means.

quiz.q: What is pandas?
options: A Python library for working with tables of data
quiz.explain: pandas gives you DataFrames: tables you can sort, filter and summarise with a few lines of code.

quiz.q: What is a Jupyter Notebook?
options: A tool where you run Python code in cells and see results, charts and notes together
quiz.explain: Jupyter lets you write code in cells, run them one by one, and see tables and charts right below the code.

days.title: Python Refresher for Data
days.goal: Refresh the Python you need: variables, lists, loops and functions.

video.title: Pandas Full Course: Basic to Advanced

steps: Make a list of numbers and use a for loop to print each one.
Write a function that takes a list and returns its average.
Use a dictionary to store a person's name, age and city.
Import the csv module and read the first three rows of a small CSV file.
days.task: Write a small script that reads a list of test scores and prints the average, highest and lowest.
days.challenge: Read a CSV file and print how many rows it has.

quiz.q: What is a list in Python?
options: An ordered collection of items, like [1, 2, 3]
quiz.explain: A list holds items in order. You read them by position, starting at 0.

quiz.q: What does a function do?
options: It groups code you can run again and again with different inputs
quiz.explain: A function bundles steps together. You call it by name whenever you need that job done.

quiz.q: What is a CSV file?
options: A text file where values are separated by commas, like a simple spreadsheet
quiz.explain: CSV stands for comma-separated values. Each line is a row and commas split the columns.

days.title: Your First DataFrame
days.goal: Load data into a pandas DataFrame and look at it.

video.title: Data Analysis with Python - Full Course for Beginners (Numpy, Pandas, Matplotlib, Seaborn)

steps: Download a small CSV dataset, like a list of movies or sales.
Load it with pd.read_csv('file.csv') into a variable called df.
Print df.head() to see the first five rows.
Print df.shape to see how many rows and columns it has.
days.task: Load a dataset of your choice and print its first five rows, its shape and its column names.
days.challenge: Load the same file and print the last five rows with df.tail().

quiz.q: What is a DataFrame?
options: A table of data with rows and columns, like a spreadsheet in Python
quiz.explain: A DataFrame is pandas' table. Rows are records, columns are fields, and you can filter and summarise them.

quiz.q: What does pd.read_csv() do?
options: It reads a CSV file into a DataFrame
quiz.explain: read_csv loads a CSV file and turns it into a DataFrame you can work with.

quiz.q: What does df.head() show?
options: The first five rows of the DataFrame
quiz.explain: head() shows the first five rows, which is a quick way to check your data loaded correctly.

days.title: Selecting Columns and Rows
days.goal: Pick out the columns and rows you need from a DataFrame.

video.title: Pandas Full Course (2025)

steps: Select one column with df['price'] and print it.
Select two columns with df[['name', 'price']] and print them.
Select the first three rows with df.iloc[0:3].
Select rows by a label with df.loc[0] and print the result.
days.task: From your dataset, show only the name and price columns for the first ten rows.
days.challenge: Select the row with the highest price using sorting, then print it.

quiz.q: How do you select one column?
quiz.explain: Square brackets with the column name give you that column as a Series.

quiz.q: What is the difference between loc and iloc?
options: loc uses labels, iloc uses positions (numbers)
quiz.explain: loc selects by label, like a name or index value. iloc selects by position number.

quiz.q: What does df[['a', 'b']] return?
options: A new DataFrame with just columns a and b
quiz.explain: Double brackets with a list of names return a DataFrame with only those columns.

days.title: Filtering Data
days.goal: Filter rows with conditions to find exactly the data you want.

video.title: Learn Pandas & Python for Data Analysis [Full Course]

steps: Filter rows where price is greater than 100 with df[df['price'] > 100].
Combine two conditions with & so both must be true.
Filter rows where the category equals 'Books'.
Count how many rows match your filter with len().
days.task: Find all products in your dataset that cost more than 5000 and are in stock.
days.challenge: Find all rows where the city is Lagos or Abuja.

quiz.q: What does df[df['price'] > 100] do?
options: It returns only the rows where price is greater than 100
quiz.explain: A condition inside square brackets filters the DataFrame to just the rows that pass the test.

quiz.q: What does & do between two conditions?
options: AND: both conditions must be true
quiz.explain: & means AND. Both sides must be true for a row to be kept.

quiz.q: Why put each condition in brackets when using &?
options: Because & has higher priority than > and =, so brackets keep the logic right
quiz.explain: Without brackets, & would bind first and the comparison would break. Always bracket each condition.

days.title: Sorting and Ranking
days.goal: Sort data to find the biggest, smallest and most recent values.

video.title: Data Visualization in Python | Matplotlib & Seaborn Tutorial for Beginners

steps: Sort your data by price from highest to lowest with sort_values().
Sort by two columns: first by category, then by price.
Use .nlargest(5, 'price') to get the five most expensive items.
Reset the index after sorting with reset_index(drop=True).
days.task: List the top 10 most expensive products and the 10 cheapest in your dataset.
days.challenge: Sort your data by date and find the most recent record.

quiz.q: What does sort_values('price', ascending=False) do?
options: It sorts rows from the highest price to the lowest
It sorts from lowest to highest
quiz.explain: ascending=False sorts from big to small. ascending=True (the default) sorts from small to big.

quiz.q: What does nlargest(5, 'price') return?
quiz.explain: nlargest(n, column) returns the n rows with the biggest values in that column.

quiz.q: Why reset the index after sorting?
options: So the row numbers run 0, 1, 2 again in the new order instead of keeping old positions
quiz.explain: After sorting, the old index stays attached. reset_index gives clean new numbers.

days.title: Project 1: Explore a Real Dataset
days.goal: Explore a real dataset end to end: load it, look at it, filter it and summarise it.

video.title: Data Visualization for Beginners, with Seaborn

steps: Pick a real CSV dataset with at least 100 rows and 4 columns.
Load it, print its shape, column names and first five rows.
Check for missing values and print how many each column has.
Filter, sort and group the data to answer three questions about it.
days.task: Finish the exploration and write a short summary of three things you found.
days.challenge: Find the most surprising fact in your dataset and write one sentence about it.

quiz.q: What should you do first with a new dataset?
options: Look at it: shape, columns, first rows and missing values
quiz.explain: First look at your data. You need to know what you have before you can analyse it.

quiz.q: Why check for missing values?
options: Because missing data can break calculations and mislead your answers
quiz.explain: Missing values can skew averages and break charts. You must know they are there before you decide what to do.

quiz.q: What is a good exploration summary?
options: A few clear findings with numbers that answer real questions
quiz.explain: A good summary gives clear findings with numbers that answer the questions you asked.

project.title: Explore a Real Dataset
project.brief: Pick a real CSV dataset with at least 100 rows and 4 columns. Load it, look at it, check missing values, filter and sort it, and write a short summary of three things you found.
checks: The dataset has at least 100 rows and 4 columns.
You printed its shape, column names and first five rows.
You counted missing values in each column.
You filtered and sorted the data to answer three questions.
Your summary has three findings, each with a number.
Your code runs without errors in a notebook.

days.title: Handling Missing Data
days.goal: Find missing values and decide what to do with them.

video.title: Matplotlib Line Charts Tutorial

steps: Use df.isna().sum() to count missing values in each column.
Drop rows with missing values using dropna() and check the new shape.
Fill missing numbers with the column average using fillna().
Fill missing text with a word like 'Unknown'.
days.task: Clean a dataset: count missing values, fill the ones you can and drop the rest.
days.challenge: Compare the average of a column before and after filling missing values.

quiz.q: What does NaN mean?
options: Not a Number: a missing value
quiz.explain: NaN marks a missing value. It is not zero; it means 'we do not have this value'.

quiz.q: When should you drop rows with missing values?
options: When only a few rows are missing and the rest of the data is still useful
quiz.explain: Dropping is fine when few rows are affected. If many rows are missing, dropping can destroy your data.

quiz.q: Why fill missing numbers with the average?
options: It keeps the row usable without changing the overall average much
quiz.explain: Filling with the average keeps the row and barely moves the column's average, which is a safe default.

days.title: Cleaning Messy Data
days.goal: Fix messy data: wrong types, extra spaces and duplicate rows.

video.title: Matplotlib Scatter Plots Tutorial

steps: Strip extra spaces from text with .str.strip().
Turn a text column of numbers into real numbers with pd.to_numeric().
Fix dates with pd.to_datetime() so you can sort and filter by date.
Remove duplicate rows with drop_duplicates() and check the new shape.
days.task: Clean a messy dataset: fix types, strip spaces, fix dates and remove duplicates.
days.challenge: Find and fix at least three different kinds of mess in your dataset.

quiz.q: Why strip spaces from text?
options: Because ' Lagos' and 'Lagos' look the same to us but are different values to Python
quiz.explain: Extra spaces make the same word count as two different values, which breaks grouping and filtering.

quiz.q: What does pd.to_numeric() do?
options: It turns text that looks like numbers into real numbers
quiz.explain: to_numeric converts a column of number-like text into numbers you can calculate with.

quiz.q: Why remove duplicates?
options: Because counting the same row twice inflates your results
quiz.explain: Duplicate rows double-count the same record, which skews totals and averages.

days.title: Grouping and Aggregating
days.goal: Group rows and calculate totals, averages and counts per group.

video.title: Matplotlib Legends Tutorial

steps: Use df.groupby('category')['price'].mean() to get the average price per category.
Use .sum() and .count() to get totals and counts per group.
Group by two columns, like category and city.
Use .agg() to calculate several things at once.
days.task: Find the average price, total sales and number of products for each category in your dataset.
days.challenge: Group your data by month and find which month had the highest sales.

quiz.q: What does groupby do?
options: It splits rows into groups by a column's values so you can calculate per group
quiz.explain: groupby splits the data into groups, like one group per category, then you calculate on each group.

quiz.q: What is an aggregate function?
options: A function that turns many values into one, like sum, mean or count
quiz.explain: Aggregates summarise many values into one number: total, average, count, biggest or smallest.

quiz.q: What does .agg(['mean', 'sum']) do?
options: It calculates both the mean and the sum in one step
quiz.explain: agg() lets you run several aggregate functions at once on the same group.

days.title: Working with Dates
days.goal: Work with dates: parse them, extract parts and filter by time.

video.title: Matplotlib Histograms Tutorial

steps: Turn a text column into dates with pd.to_datetime().
Extract the year, month and day into new columns.
Filter rows to only those after a certain date.
Group by month and count how many records fall in each month.
days.task: From a dataset with dates, find the busiest month and the quietest month.
days.challenge: Calculate the number of days between two dates in your data.

quiz.q: Why turn text into dates with to_datetime()?
options: So you can sort, filter and do maths with dates
quiz.explain: As text, dates are just words. As dates, you can compare them, sort them and subtract them.

quiz.q: How do you get the month from a date column?
quiz.explain: The .dt accessor gives you parts of a date, like .dt.month, .dt.year and .dt.day.

quiz.q: What does resample('M') do?
options: It groups time data by month
quiz.explain: resample('M') groups a time series into months so you can calculate per month.

days.title: Combining DataFrames
days.goal: Join tables together with merge and stack them with concat.

video.title: Matplotlib 3D Plots Tutorial

steps: Load two related CSV files, like products and sales.
Merge them on a shared column with pd.merge().
Try an inner join and a left join and compare the row counts.
Stack two DataFrames with the same columns using pd.concat().
days.task: Join a products table and a sales table, then find total sales per product.
days.challenge: Merge two tables and find which rows have no match in the other table.

quiz.q: What does pd.merge() do?
options: It joins two DataFrames on a shared column, like a database join
quiz.explain: merge combines two tables using a column they share, like a product id.

quiz.q: What is the difference between an inner join and a left join?
options: Inner keeps only rows with a match in both tables. Left keeps all rows from the left table
quiz.explain: Inner join keeps only matches. Left join keeps every left row and fills missing right values with NaN.

quiz.q: What does pd.concat() do?
options: It stacks DataFrames on top of each other
quiz.explain: concat stacks tables vertically when they have the same columns.

days.title: Pivot Tables
days.goal: Summarise data in a grid with pivot tables.

video.title: Matplotlib 3D Plots Advanced Tutorial

steps: Make a pivot table with rows as category and columns as city.
Use values='sales' and aggfunc='sum' to total sales in each cell.
Add margins=True to see row and column totals.
Use a pivot table to compare sales across months and categories.
days.task: Build a pivot table of sales by product category and month.
days.challenge: Find the best-selling category in each city using a pivot table.

quiz.q: What is a pivot table?
options: A summary grid that shows an aggregate for each combination of row and column values
quiz.explain: A pivot table turns long data into a grid, like sales by category (rows) and city (columns).

quiz.q: What does aggfunc do in a pivot table?
options: It decides how values combine in each cell, like sum or mean
quiz.explain: aggfunc picks the calculation for each cell, such as sum, mean or count.

quiz.q: What does margins=True add?
options: Row and column totals at the edges of the table
quiz.explain: margins adds a Total row and column so you can see the overall numbers at a glance.

days.title: Project 2: Sales Analysis Report
days.goal: Analyse a sales dataset end to end and write a short report with numbers.

video.title: Matplotlib Animations Tutorial

steps: Pick a sales dataset with products, categories, dates and amounts.
Clean it: fix types, handle missing values and remove duplicates.
Group and pivot the data to answer: best category, best month, best city.
Write a short report with your findings and the numbers behind them.
days.task: Finish the sales report with at least three findings, each with a number.
days.challenge: Add one chart to your report that supports your main finding.

quiz.q: What makes a good analysis report?
options: Clear findings, each backed by a number, and a short explanation of what it means
quiz.explain: A good report gives clear findings with numbers and explains what each number means for the business.

quiz.q: Why clean data before analysing it?
options: Because dirty data gives wrong answers
quiz.explain: Analysis on dirty data gives wrong totals and averages. Clean first, analyse second.

quiz.q: How do you pick the main finding?
options: The finding that matters most for the decision the report supports
quiz.explain: The main finding is the one that changes what someone should do next.

project.title: Sales Analysis Report
project.brief: Analyse a sales dataset end to end: clean it, group and pivot it to find the best category, month and city, and write a short report with your findings and the numbers behind them.
checks: The data is cleaned: types fixed, missing values handled, duplicates removed.
You found the best category by total sales.
You found the best month and the best city.
Your report has at least three findings with numbers.
Your report includes at least one chart.
Your report explains what the findings mean for the business.

days.title: Introduction to Matplotlib
days.goal: Draw your first charts with Matplotlib.

video.title: Complete Data Visualization Course for Beginners | Matplotlib & Seaborn

steps: Make a line chart of monthly sales with plt.plot().
Add a title, x-label and y-label to the chart.
Make a bar chart of sales by category.
Save the chart to a file with plt.savefig().
days.task: Draw a line chart of sales over time and a bar chart of sales by category.
days.challenge: Change the chart colours and add a grid to make it easier to read.

quiz.q: What is Matplotlib?
options: Python's main charting library for drawing line, bar and scatter charts
quiz.explain: Matplotlib draws charts. You give it data and it draws lines, bars and points.

quiz.q: What does plt.plot(x, y) do?
options: It draws a line chart connecting the points
quiz.explain: plot() draws a line through your x and y values, which is good for showing change over time.

quiz.q: Why add labels and a title to a chart?
options: So anyone can understand what the chart shows without asking you
quiz.explain: Labels and titles tell the reader what the axes mean and what the chart is about.

days.title: Bar Charts and Histograms
days.goal: Show comparisons with bar charts and distributions with histograms.

video.title: Data visualization - Matplotlib vs Seaborn vs Plotly

steps: Make a horizontal bar chart of the top 10 products.
Make a histogram of prices to see how they are spread out.
Add value labels on top of bars so readers can see exact numbers.
Use different colours to highlight the biggest bar.
days.task: Draw a bar chart of your top 5 categories and a histogram of a numeric column.
days.challenge: Make a histogram with 20 bins and compare it with one that has 5 bins.

quiz.q: When is a bar chart the right choice?
quiz.explain: Bar charts compare amounts across categories, like sales per product or per city.

quiz.q: What does a histogram show?
options: How values are spread out: how many fall into each range
quiz.explain: A histogram groups numbers into bins and shows how many fall in each bin, revealing the shape of the data.

quiz.q: What happens when you use more bins in a histogram?
options: You see more detail in the shape, but it can get noisy
quiz.explain: More bins show finer detail. Too many bins make the chart noisy and hard to read.

days.title: Line Charts and Trends
days.goal: Show change over time with line charts and spot trends.

video.title: Weather Data Analysis with Python Pandas: Real Project Walkthrough

steps: Plot daily or monthly values as a line chart.
Add a second line to compare two products over time.
Use a rolling average to smooth a noisy line.
Mark the highest and lowest points on the chart.
days.task: Draw a line chart of sales over 12 months and add a 3-month rolling average.
days.challenge: Compare two products on one chart and say which one is growing faster.

quiz.q: When is a line chart the right choice?
options: For showing how values change over time
quiz.explain: Line charts connect points in time order, which makes trends and patterns easy to see.

quiz.q: What is a rolling average?
options: The average of the last few points, recalculated at each step, which smooths noise
quiz.explain: A rolling average averages a small window of recent points, which smooths out daily noise and shows the trend.

quiz.q: Why compare two lines on one chart?
options: So you can see which one grows faster and when they cross
quiz.explain: Two lines on one chart make it easy to compare growth and spot when one overtakes the other.

days.title: Scatter Plots and Relationships
days.goal: Show relationships between two numbers with scatter plots.

video.title: Star Wars Survey Analysis Using Python

steps: Plot price against sales as a scatter plot.
Colour the points by category to see groups.
Add a trend line to see the general direction.
Look for outliers: points far from the rest.
days.task: Draw a scatter plot of two numeric columns in your data and describe the relationship.
days.challenge: Find one outlier in your data and check if it is a real value or a mistake.

quiz.q: What does a scatter plot show?
options: How two numbers relate to each other, one point per row
quiz.explain: A scatter plot puts one number on each axis. Each dot is a row, and the pattern shows the relationship.

quiz.q: What is an outlier?
options: A point far from the rest of the data
quiz.explain: An outlier is a value far from the others. It may be a mistake, or it may be the most interesting point.

quiz.q: What does a trend line show?
options: The general direction of the relationship
quiz.explain: A trend line summarises the direction: as one value grows, does the other grow, shrink or stay flat?

days.title: Seaborn for Better Charts
days.goal: Make prettier, more informative charts with Seaborn.

video.title: Million Songs Dataset Analysis using Python

steps: Make a bar chart with sns.barplot() and compare it with Matplotlib's.
Make a box plot to see the spread of values in each category.
Make a heatmap of a correlation matrix.
Set a Seaborn theme to make all your charts look consistent.
days.task: Redraw your best chart with Seaborn and compare it with the Matplotlib version.
days.challenge: Make a box plot that shows which category has the most spread-out prices.

quiz.q: What is Seaborn?
options: A charting library built on Matplotlib that makes nicer statistical charts with less code
quiz.explain: Seaborn sits on top of Matplotlib. It draws statistical charts like box plots and heatmaps with short code.

quiz.q: What does a box plot show?
options: The spread of values: median, quartiles and outliers
quiz.explain: A box plot shows the middle half of the data as a box, the median as a line, and outliers as dots.

quiz.q: What is a correlation matrix?
options: A table showing how strongly each pair of numbers moves together
quiz.explain: A correlation matrix shows, for every pair of numeric columns, whether they rise together, fall together or are unrelated.

days.title: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
days.goal: Do a full EDA: describe, visualise and question a dataset.

video.title: Exploratory Data Analysis: Vienna Hotels Part 1

steps: Run df.describe() to get counts, means and quartiles for numeric columns.
Check the data types and missing values for every column.
Draw a chart for each key column: a histogram for numbers, a bar chart for categories.
Write down five questions the data can answer and five it cannot.
days.task: Do a full EDA on a new dataset and write a one-page summary of what you found.
days.challenge: Find one relationship in the data that surprises you and check it with a chart.

quiz.q: What is EDA?
options: Exploring a dataset with summaries and charts to understand it before formal analysis
quiz.explain: EDA is the first look: describe, plot and question the data so you understand it before you analyse it deeply.

quiz.q: What does df.describe() give you?
options: Counts, means, standard deviations, minimums and quartiles for numeric columns
quiz.explain: describe() summarises each numeric column: how many values, the average, the spread and the quartiles.

quiz.q: Why write down what the data cannot answer?
options: So you do not claim answers the data does not support
quiz.explain: Knowing the limits stops you from overclaiming. Honest analysis says what it cannot prove.

days.title: Project 3: Full EDA and Dashboard Charts
days.goal: Do a complete EDA on a real dataset and present it as a set of charts.

video.title: Exploratory Data Analysis: Vienna Hotels Part 2

steps: Pick a dataset you have not used before, with at least 500 rows.
Clean it and run a full EDA with describe() and charts for each key column.
Make at least five charts: line, bar, histogram, scatter and one more of your choice.
Write a short findings document with your charts and three key insights.
days.task: Finish the EDA document with five charts and three insights.
days.challenge: Present your findings to one person in under three minutes.

quiz.q: What makes a good EDA document?
options: Clear questions, clean data, honest charts and findings with numbers
quiz.explain: A good EDA asks clear questions, shows clean data and charts, and gives findings backed by numbers.

quiz.q: How many charts should an EDA have?
options: Enough to answer the questions: usually one per key column or relationship
quiz.explain: Each chart should answer a question. Extra charts that answer nothing only add noise.

quiz.q: Why present your findings out loud?
options: Because explaining forces you to be clear, and questions reveal gaps
quiz.explain: Presenting tests your understanding. If you cannot explain a finding simply, you do not fully understand it yet.

project.title: Full EDA and Dashboard Charts
project.brief: Do a complete exploratory data analysis on a real dataset with at least 500 rows. Clean it, describe it, make at least five charts (line, bar, histogram, scatter and one more), and write a findings document with three key insights.
checks: The dataset has at least 500 rows.
You cleaned the data and ran df.describe().
You made at least five charts of different types.
Each chart has a title and labels.
Your document has three key insights with numbers.
You can present your findings in under three minutes.

days.title: Working with Real Datasets
days.goal: Find and load real datasets from public sources.

video.title: Exploratory Data Analysis: Vienna Hotels Part 3

steps: Download a dataset from Kaggle or a public data portal.
Load it and check its shape, columns and missing values.
Read the dataset's description to understand what each column means.
Pick one question the dataset can answer and plan your analysis.
days.task: Find a dataset about a topic you care about and write down three questions it can answer.
days.challenge: Load the dataset and check whether it is clean or messy.

quiz.q: Where can you find real datasets?
options: Kaggle, public data portals, government open data sites and company data pages
quiz.explain: Kaggle, data.gov and other open data portals host thousands of free real datasets.

quiz.q: Why read the dataset description first?
options: So you know what each column means and what the data can and cannot tell you
quiz.explain: The description tells you what the columns mean, how the data was collected and what its limits are.

quiz.q: What makes a dataset good for practice?
options: It has a clear topic, enough rows, and a mix of numbers, categories and dates
quiz.explain: A good practice dataset is big enough to explore, has mixed column types, and a topic you care about.

days.title: Statistics for Analysts
days.goal: Use the statistics that matter: mean, median, mode and standard deviation.

video.title: Mall Customer Segmentation Analysis using Python

steps: Calculate the mean, median and mode of a column and compare them.
Calculate the standard deviation to see how spread out values are.
Use percentiles to find the value that 90% of rows fall below.
Explain in plain words what each number means for your data.
days.task: Calculate mean, median and standard deviation for three columns and explain each in one sentence.
days.challenge: Find a column where the mean and median are very different and explain why.

quiz.q: What is the median?
options: The middle value when data is sorted
quiz.explain: The median is the middle value. Half the data is below it and half above it.

quiz.q: When is the median better than the mean?
options: When a few huge values would pull the mean up and mislead you
quiz.explain: The mean is pulled by outliers. The median stays in the middle, so it describes typical values better when data is skewed.

quiz.q: What does standard deviation measure?
options: How spread out values are around the mean
quiz.explain: Standard deviation measures spread. A small value means data clusters near the mean; a big value means it is spread out.

days.title: Correlation and What It Does Not Prove
days.goal: Measure correlation and learn why it does not prove cause.

video.title: Iris Dataset Analysis using Python

steps: Calculate a correlation matrix with df.corr() for numeric columns.
Draw a heatmap of the correlations.
Find the strongest positive and strongest negative correlation.
Write one sentence for each: what it shows and what it does not prove.
days.task: Find the strongest correlation in your dataset and explain it without claiming cause.
days.challenge: Find two columns that look related but probably are not, and explain why.

quiz.q: What does a correlation of 0.9 mean?
options: The two values rise together strongly
quiz.explain: A correlation near 1 means the values move together. Near -1 means they move in opposite directions. Near 0 means no clear link.

quiz.q: Why does correlation not prove causation?
options: Because a third factor may cause both, or the link may be coincidence
quiz.explain: Two things can rise together because a third thing drives both. Correlation shows a link, not a cause.

quiz.q: What is a heatmap good for?
options: Showing a whole correlation matrix at a glance with colour
quiz.explain: A heatmap colours each cell by value, so strong and weak correlations jump out at a glance.

days.title: Telling Stories with Data
days.goal: Turn findings into a story people remember and act on.

video.title: Data Analysis with Python for Excel Users - Full Course

steps: Pick one main message from your analysis.
Order your charts so each one builds on the last.
Write a headline for each chart in plain words.
End with a clear recommendation: what should happen next.
days.task: Turn your sales analysis into a three-chart story with a recommendation.
days.challenge: Rewrite one chart title so a non-technical person understands it instantly.

quiz.q: What is data storytelling?
options: Presenting findings as a clear story: context, evidence, and what to do next
quiz.explain: Data storytelling turns numbers into a narrative people can follow and act on.

quiz.q: Why order charts like a story?
options: So each chart builds on the last and the reader follows your thinking
quiz.explain: Ordered charts guide the reader from the problem to the evidence to the recommendation.

quiz.q: What makes a good chart title?
options: A plain sentence that states the finding, like 'Sales doubled in December'
quiz.explain: A good title states the finding in plain words, so the reader gets the point before reading the chart.

days.title: Building a Simple Dashboard
days.goal: Build a small dashboard that shows key numbers and charts together.

video.title: Pandas Full Course: Basic to Advanced

steps: Pick three key numbers (KPIs) for your dataset and show them at the top.
Add three charts below: one trend, one comparison and one distribution.
Arrange them in a clean layout in a Jupyter Notebook or a simple web page.
Add a short line under each chart explaining what it shows.
days.task: Build a one-page dashboard for your sales dataset with three KPIs and three charts.
days.challenge: Show your dashboard to one person and ask them what they understand from it.

quiz.q: What is a KPI?
options: A key performance indicator: a single number that shows how something important is doing
quiz.explain: A KPI is one number that matters, like total sales or average order value, shown big and clear.

quiz.q: What makes a good dashboard?
options: A few key numbers and charts that answer the main questions at a glance
quiz.explain: A good dashboard answers the main questions in seconds. Too many charts hide the important ones.

quiz.q: Why add a short line under each chart?
options: So the reader knows what the chart shows and why it matters
quiz.explain: A short caption tells the reader what to look for, so they do not have to guess.

days.title: Presenting Your Analysis
days.goal: Present your work clearly to people who are not analysts.

video.title: Data Analysis with Python - Full Course for Beginners (Numpy, Pandas, Matplotlib, Seaborn)

steps: Write a one-page summary: the question, the answer and the evidence.
Pick your three best charts and give each a plain-words title.
Practise explaining your findings in under five minutes.
Prepare for two questions people might ask and write your answers.
days.task: Write a one-page summary of your best analysis and practise presenting it.
days.challenge: Present it to one person and note their questions.

quiz.q: What should a one-page summary contain?
options: The question, the answer, the key numbers and what should happen next
quiz.explain: A one-page summary gives the question, the answer, the evidence and the next step, nothing more.

quiz.q: Why practise presenting?
options: Because explaining simply proves you understand it and reveals gaps
quiz.explain: Presenting tests your understanding. If you cannot explain a finding simply, you do not fully understand it yet.

quiz.q: How should you handle a question you cannot answer?
options: Say you do not know and offer to check
quiz.explain: Saying 'I don't know, I'll check' is honest and builds trust. Guessing destroys it.

days.title: Working with Excel Files
days.goal: Read and write Excel files with pandas.

video.title: Pandas Full Course (2025)

steps: Install openpyxl with pip install openpyxl.
Read an Excel file with pd.read_excel('data.xlsx').
Write a DataFrame to Excel with df.to_excel('output.xlsx', index=False).
Write two sheets into one Excel file using ExcelWriter.
days.task: Read a sales spreadsheet from Excel, clean it, and save the cleaned version to a new file.
days.challenge: Write a summary table and a chart-ready table to two sheets of one Excel file.

quiz.q: What does pd.read_excel() do?
options: It reads an Excel spreadsheet into a DataFrame
quiz.explain: read_excel loads an Excel sheet into a DataFrame, just like read_csv does for CSV files.

quiz.q: Why use index=False when writing to Excel?
options: So pandas does not add an extra index column to your spreadsheet
quiz.explain: Without index=False, pandas writes the row numbers as an extra column, which clutters the spreadsheet.

quiz.q: What is ExcelWriter for?
options: Writing several DataFrames to different sheets of one Excel file
quiz.explain: ExcelWriter lets you write multiple sheets into a single workbook in one go.

days.title: Automating Reports with Python
days.goal: Turn your analysis into a script that runs the whole report by itself.

video.title: Learn Pandas & Python for Data Analysis [Full Course]

steps: Put your cleaning, grouping and chart steps into one Python script.
Make the script read the latest data file and save the charts to a folder.
Run the script from the terminal with python report.py.
Schedule it to run every week, or run it by hand when new data arrives.
days.task: Turn your sales analysis into a single script that produces the charts and the numbers in one run.
days.challenge: Add a line at the end of the script that prints 'Report done' with today's date.

quiz.q: What is an automated report?
options: A script that loads fresh data, analyses it and produces charts and numbers without you doing each step
quiz.explain: An automated report script does the whole job: load, clean, analyse and chart, so you run one command and get the results.

quiz.q: Why put analysis in a script instead of a notebook?
options: So the same steps run the same way every time, with no missed steps
quiz.explain: A script runs top to bottom the same way every time, which makes results repeatable and easy to schedule.

quiz.q: What should a report script print at the end?
options: A short summary: what it did, how many rows it used and where the outputs are
quiz.explain: A short summary at the end tells you the run worked and where to find the results.

days.title: Capstone Prep: Plan Your Analysis
days.goal: Review everything, pick your capstone dataset and plan your report.

video.title: Data Visualization in Python | Matplotlib & Seaborn Tutorial for Beginners

steps: List the datasets you worked with and pick the most interesting one.
Write a short plan: the questions, the data, the charts and the report.
Practise explaining your analysis in simple words, as if to a friend.
Record a short video or write a short post showing your dashboard.
days.task: Write your capstone plan and a one-minute explanation of your analysis.
days.challenge: Show your dashboard to one person and note their questions, then improve it.

quiz.q: What makes a good capstone analysis?
options: A real question, clean data, honest charts and a clear recommendation
quiz.explain: A good capstone answers a real question with clean data, honest charts and a recommendation someone can act on.

quiz.q: Why practise explaining your analysis?
options: Because explaining simply proves you truly understand it
quiz.explain: If you can explain your analysis in simple words, you really understand it. That is what employers look for.

quiz.q: What should your capstone plan include?
options: The questions, the data, the charts, the report and how you will show it
quiz.explain: A plan covers the questions you will answer, the data you will use, the charts you will make and how you will present it.

capstone.title: Analyse a Real Dataset and Present a Dashboard
capstone.brief: Pick a real dataset about a topic you care about. Clean it, explore it, find answers to real questions, and build a one-page dashboard with KPIs and charts. Write a short report with your findings and a recommendation, and present it in a short video or live demo.
checks: The analysis answers a real question and you can state the question in one sentence.
The data is cleaned and the cleaning steps are explained.
The dashboard has at least three KPIs and three charts.
Each chart has a plain-words title and a short caption.
The report has at least three findings, each with a number.
The report ends with a clear recommendation.
You can present your analysis in under five minutes in simple words.
deliverables: A cleaned dataset and the notebook with your analysis.
A one-page dashboard with KPIs and charts.
A short written report with findings and a recommendation.
A short demo video or screenshots of your dashboard.
A one-page write-up of what you learned in 30 days.
